question_text: How does a laboratory analysis of a wine help the quality control manager make decisions at bottling?
command_word_demand: An explanatory/analytical 'how', with an implied 'why' behind every analysis: "A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part which is implied in the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked any analytical depth." The answer had to be about quality control decisions, not a description of bottling: "Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question…"

required_elements.element: State the objective bottling QC serves — a wine that reaches the consumer palatable, typical, stable, fault- and contaminant-free, and legally compliant, with bottling as the last chance to adjust
required_elements.quote: To ensure that the wine reaches the consumer in a state which is palatable, typical and stable; free from faults and contaminants; and compliant with all relevant legislation and regulation. Bottling is a key step in ensuring this and is the last opportunity to make adjustments.

required_elements.element: Treat lab analysis as a decision tool and name the decisions it drives — final filtration, additives, microbial stability, hazes — saying why and what action follows
required_elements.quote: Lab analysis is a tool that provides relevant technical information to allow appropriate decisions about treatments and handling (candidates should show an understanding of what these might be - to cover final filtration, additives, microbial stability, hazes, why and what action might be taken).

required_elements.element: Cover the packaging process and dry goods, and compliance with product specification, not just the wine itself
required_elements.quote: Candidates needed to consider both quality checks on wine and checks on the packaging process and dry goods, as well as … compliance with product specification.

required_elements.element: Answer the implied 'why' each analysis is carried out, rather than listing analyses
required_elements.quote: A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part which is implied in the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked any analytical depth.

required_elements.element: Address safety of staff handling liquid and packaging (broken glass, noise, heavy lifting, health risks)
required_elements.quote: The safety of staff handling the liquid and the packaging is also critical (with risks such as broken glass, noise, heavy lifting and exposure to health risks).

required_elements.element: Bring in HACCP and critical control points
required_elements.quote: Consideration of HACCP and critical control points is always useful in a question that mentions bottling.

required_elements.element: Frame QC inside quality assurance and food-law compliance, showing awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements
required_elements.quote: Quality control is part of the overall quality assurance process, and wine is a foodstuff which must comply with legislative and regulatory standards (so an awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements is helpful).

required_elements.element: Spell out the consequences of getting it wrong — loss of quality, consumer disappointment, brand damage, recall or unsaleable-stock costs
required_elements.quote: Issues for the wine itself include loss of quality, consumer disappointment, damage to brand, and costs attached to issuing recalls or being unable to sell the wine.

credit_signals.signal: Used many examples and quotes from industry leaders, and worked through the points analytically rather than descriptively (paper-level General Observations)
credit_signals.quote: Good candidates used lots of examples and quotes from industry leaders. They worked through a logical list of the risks and benefits and demonstrated analysis of the points they were making, comparing and contrasting, and discussing.

credit_signals.signal: Opened with an introduction summarising the question and the ground to be covered (paper-level General Observations)
credit_signals.quote: It has been said before, but it is worth repeating, that a good introduction should summarise understanding of the question and ground to be covered, as this will help candidates focus and would have improved answers in many cases.

penalty_signals.signal: Described the bottling process instead of addressing quality control, and showed no awareness of the key QC analyses or their purpose
penalty_signals.quote: Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question and showed lack of awareness of key QC analyses for wine and why they are carried out.

penalty_signals.signal: Unfocused answers that omitted too much of the expected content
penalty_signals.quote: A number of candidates lacked focus or simply missed too many key issues.

penalty_signals.signal: WSET-style descriptive answers with no 'how' or 'why' and no analysis (paper-level)
penalty_signals.quote: One complaint from examiners was that many candidates were too simplistic in their answers, giving WSET-type descriptive answers and not explaining "how" or "why" nor showing any analysis.

penalty_signals.signal: Vague quantities instead of actual figures; loose use of 'sulphur' for sulphites/SO2 (paper-level)
penalty_signals.quote: Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required. Inaccurate use of "sulphur" instead of sulphites or sulphur dioxide still crops up regularly…

examples_expected.specificity: Real numbers and real-world practical detail, not vague statements — the paper preamble names EU SO2 limits (and whether free or total), typical free SO2 levels by style, actual pH values, permitted and actual additive usage levels, and filtration pore sizes as the kind of factual/numerical knowledge expected. No question-specific examples were named by the report.
examples_expected.quote: Paper 3 is a technical paper and it is expected that candidates will have a firm grasp of some key factual and numerical information. EU limits for SO2 use, being clear about the whether numbers refer to total or free SO2; typical levels of free SO2 for various styles; actual values for pH; permitted and actual usage levels for common wine additives; pore sizes for filtration and so on are key knowledge for MWs.

scope_traps.trap: Reading the question as 'describe bottling' rather than 'what does lab analysis let the QC manager decide'
scope_traps.quote: Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question…

scope_traps.trap: Writing what you know about the topic instead of answering the question as set (paper-level)
scope_traps.quote: Many candidates failed to answer at least part of the question as set and were tempted into simply writing what they knew about a topic.

performance_note: No question-level attempt or pass figures given. Paper-level: "Paper 3 had a relatively high pass rate of close to 50% in 2018…". For this question, "A number of candidates lacked focus or simply missed too many key issues."
extraction_notes: Commentary is anchored on verbatim question text (match 1.0). The examiners' 'Key understanding' block supplied most required_elements; the prose below it supplied the penalty signals. Four items (two credit_signals, one penalty_signal, one scope_trap, and examples_expected) are drawn from the Paper 3 paper-level General Observations by Caroline Gilby MW, not from this question's own commentary — they apply paper-wide. An OCR page number ('17') sits inside the product-specification sentence and has been elided with '…'.

question_text: Describe the options available for bulk transport of wine. What are the risks and benefits for each option?
command_word: Describe … What are the risks and benefits for each option?
command_word_demand: A two-part demand: describe the options, then analyse risks and benefits option by option — general discussion of the topic did not satisfy it. "Another issue was candidates writing generalised and descriptive answers around the topic of bulk transport without specifically analysing each option." The examiners rewarded "a logical list of the risks and benefits" with "analysis of the points they were making, comparing and contrasting and discussing."

definitions_required.quote: They failed to define the key words in the question and therefore went "off piste" from the start. Interpretation of the phrase "bulk wine" should not have been difficult even for non-mother tongue English speakers.

required_elements.element: Identify the two bulk-transport systems: ISO tanks and flexitanks
required_elements.quote: For the movement of bulk wine, two systems are available - ISO tanks and Flexitanks.

required_elements.element: Describe ISO tanks technically: stainless steel, fitting standard trucks, transferable to rail or sea, one large tank or 3–4 sectional tanks
required_elements.quote: ISO tanks: stainless steel vessels designed to fit directly onto standard trucks and also transferred to be transported by rail or sea. They can be constructed as one large tank or divided up into 3 or 4 sectional tanks.

required_elements.element: Describe flexitanks technically: flexible bags in a standard 20ft container, usually single use, polyethylene with an EVOH copolymer barrier against oxygen and taint
required_elements.quote: Flexitanks: flexible bags that are fitted into a standard 20ft container. Usually used once only. The latest systems are constructed of polyethylene with a barrier material of ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) copolymer, creating an effective barrier to oxygen and to organic materials that can taint wine.

required_elements.quote: …it was surprising how many candidates did not have a basic understanding of the options and muddled up ISO tanks and flexitanks.

credit_signals.quote: Good candidates used lots of examples and quotes from industry leaders.

credit_signals.quote: They worked through a logical list of the risks and benefits and demonstrated analysis of the points they were making, comparing and contrasting and discussing.

penalty_signals.signal: Muddled ISO tanks and flexitanks / lacked basic understanding of the options

penalty_signals.signal: Failed to define the question's key words and drifted off topic from the opening
penalty_signals.quote: Several candidates misunderstood or misinterpreted the question. They failed to define the key words in the question and therefore went "off piste" from the start.

penalty_signals.signal: Spent paragraphs on bottled wine — no marks, and time lost
penalty_signals.quote: The inclusion of paragraphs on bottled wine in several answers gained no points and wasted time.

penalty_signals.signal: Generalised, descriptive coverage of bulk transport without analysing each option separately — knowledge without an answer to the question
penalty_signals.quote: Another issue was candidates writing generalised and descriptive answers around the topic of bulk transport without specifically analysing each option. It is particularly frustrating to see candidates who clearly knew a lot about bulk transport failing because they simply did not address the question.

examples_expected.specificity: Examples and quotes from industry leaders; the paper preamble also demands real numbers and practical detail and criticises narrowness of examples. The report names no specific companies, routes or figures for this question.
examples_expected.quote: Good candidates used lots of examples and quotes from industry leaders.

scope_traps.trap: Writing about bottled wine / packaged-goods transport when the question is about bulk
scope_traps.quote: The inclusion of paragraphs on bottled wine in several answers gained no points and wasted time.

scope_traps.trap: Treating it as 'write what you know about bulk transport' rather than describing the options and analysing each one's risks and benefits
scope_traps.quote: It is particularly frustrating to see candidates who clearly knew a lot about bulk transport failing because they simply did not address the question.

performance_note: No attempt or pass numbers given. The examiners record surprise at the weak grasp of a current industry topic: "Given that this is currently such a hot topic for the wine industry it was surprising how many candidates did not have a basic understanding of the options…"
extraction_notes: VERIFIED against the flag 'anchored by question number, not text'. The report abbreviated the restatement to 'Question 2: each option?' (the tail of the corpus question's second sentence), but the commentary unambiguously discusses this corpus question: it opens 'For the movement of bulk wine, two systems are available - ISO tanks and Flexitanks', discusses 'bulk wine' as the phrase to be defined, and praises candidates who 'worked through a logical list of the risks and benefits'. Coverage set to 'full' on that basis. The truncated restatement also means the report never re-states 'Describe the options available for bulk transport of wine' — command_word is taken from the corpus question_text, which is authoritative. Two credit/penalty items overlap with the Paper 3 General Observations, which repeat the industry-leader-quotes and logical-list phrasing verbatim.

extraction_notes: Commentary anchored on verbatim question text (match 1.0). The five bullet requirements come from the examiners' 'Key understanding' list; each quote reproduces the list's lead-in ('A closure should:') so the bullet is attributable, with '…' marking elision of the intervening bullets. extraction_notes: Commentary anchored on verbatim question text (match 1.0). The examiners explicitly PERMIT (but do not require) a structure that pairs the methods: "Candidates may consider depth filtration methods (a & b) as well as absolute filters (c &d) together." Recorded here rather than as a required_element because it is a permitted structure, not a demand — a grader should not penalise either structure. The differentiator is the 'so what': "The most common shortcoming was in a lack of analysis of the implications of the changes in demand - the "so what" which is where an MW candidate can really stand out."

question_text: Evaluate the extent to which scarcity/rarity is a positive attribute in wine marketing.
command_word_demand: The examiners gloss the construction plainly: "Perhaps the somewhat unusual structure of the question "examine the extent to which" put candidates off, but in effect it only means "how much"." With a narrow subject, they required command of the key points plus explicit critical thinking: "The subject matter was relatively narrow, which meant that a good understanding of the key points was essential, as was the need to deploy critical thinking skill."

extraction_notes: WORDING DISCREPANCY: the corpus question_text reads 'Evaluate the extent to which…' but the report's commentary quotes the question as 'examine the extent to which'. The corpus is authoritative (it comes from the paper); command_word is therefore recorded as 'Evaluate', with the report's gloss retained verbatim in command_word_demand since the examiners' explanation ('it only means "how much"') applies either way. credit_signals is empty because the report describes no successful answers on this question — it only records failure modes, consistent with '48 undertook this question and only a very small number passed'. Several required_elements derive from the examiners' rhetorical questions ('Is there a consumer benefit to scarcity?'); these are read as the content they expected covered, which is how the surrounding sentences frame them. An OCR page number ('22') sits inside the 'We are … really exploring' sentence and has been elided. No paper-level General Comments exist for Paper 4.
